chat-with-your-documents:
# Chat With Your Documents A local RAG document assistant — Ollama + LangChain + Chroma + Streamlit, no cloud, no API key — **built to make its own failures visible.** Implemented from Woongsik Su, *Chat With Your Documents* (Book Two, 2 August 2026). The book's thesis is the reason this repo exists: > A local RAG system does not crash. It degrades quietly and keeps answering — retrieval > brings back the wrong paragraph and the model writes something fluent from it, or the index > is empty and the pipeline reports success. So every component here either produces a grounded answer or **says why it will not**. --- ## The two quiet failures, and what this does about them | Failure | What most RAG demos do | What this does | |---|---|---| | Index is empty | Answer from the model's own knowledge. Looks fine. | Refuse. `reason="empty-index"` | | Retrieval returns junk | Feed the junk to the LLM and print fluent nonsense | Refuse if the best chunk is beyond a distance cap. `reason="below-threshold"` | Both refusals are demonstrated against real embeddings, not mocks: ``` $ python -c "from rag import answer; ..." Q: Why is accuracy a misleading metric for threshold data? refused: False distances: [0.3931, 0.4981, 0.5416, 0.6544] > Accuracy is a misleading metric ... because it does not measure how well the > model performs near the decision boundary ... Q: What was the closing share price of Toyota in 1998? refused: True reason: below-threshold distances: [1.0542, 1.0603, 1.0608, 1.0801] > Nothing in the indexed documents is close enough to that question, so I am > not going to answer it from them. ``` Nothing in the index is about Toyota. A RAG app without that distance check answers the second question anyway, and sounds just as confident as it did on the first. --- ## Modules | File | Responsibility | |---|---| | `loaders.py` | Seven extensions through one dispatch table. Running headers/footers stripped (`strip_repeated_lines`), encodings tried in order, unreadable files reported loudly rather than skipped | | `ingest.py` | Chunking (`RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter`, 500/100), embedding, Chroma persist. **Content-hash chunk ids** so re-ingesting is idempotent | | `rag.py` | `retrieve` returns distances alongside chunks; `answer()` returns an `Answer` with `refused` and `reason` | | `app.py` | Streamlit chat that shows retrieved chunks **and their distances every turn**, plus live `k` and distance-cap sliders | ```mermaid flowchart LR D[data/] --> L[loaders.py
7 formats, header strip] L --> I[ingest.py
chunk + hash id] I --> C[(Chroma
chroma_db/)] Q[question] --> R[rag.py] C --> R R -->|best distance under cap| A[grounded answer] R -->|empty index| X[refuse: empty-index] R -->|all chunks too far| Y[refuse: below-threshold] A --> U[app.py
shows chunks + distances] X --> U Y --> U ``` --- ## Run it Needs [Ollama](https://ollama.com) running locally. ```bash ollama pull nomic-embed-text # embeddings ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b # chat model python -m venv .venv .venv\Scripts\activate # Windows pip install -r requirements.txt # put documents in data/ , then python ingest.py streamlit run app.py ``` `pytest -q` — **11 tests, and they need no Ollama.** The embedder and LLM are faked, so the suite runs anywhere. --- ## Verified on this machine | | | |---|---| | Ollama | 0.32.5, `nomic-embed-text` + `qwen2.5-coder:7b` | | Versions | chromadb 1.5.9, streamlit 1.60.0 — the exact versions the book targets | | Python | 3.13.5 on Windows | | Idempotent re-ingest | 2 documents → 29 chunks; running `ingest.py` again → **still 29** | | Refusals | both paths confirmed against real embeddings (above) | | Tests | 11 passed, no daemon required | --- ## Deviations from the book See `ISSUES_FOUND.md`. The short version: the book uses `qwen3:8b`; this machine has `qwen2.5-coder:7b`, so `CHAT_MODEL` differs. And Chroma's `similarity_search_with_score` returns a **distance** for this embedding, not a similarity — so the threshold test is `min(distance) > cap`, which is the opposite comparison to what "score" suggests. --- ## What I'd improve next - Conversation memory. `answer()` accepts `history` and ignores it — the book adds this later. - Reranking. Distance alone is a blunt filter; a cross-encoder over the top 20 would be better. - Hybrid retrieval. Dense embeddings miss exact identifiers; BM25 alongside would catch them. - Calibrate the distance cap per corpus instead of the hard-coded 1.05 default. - Chunk-level evaluation — this is project #7 in the portfolio ladder, and it should run against *this* repo. --- ## Licence MIT for this implementation. The book's design and its example code remain the author's.
tiny-rag-pytorch:
# tiny-rag-pytorch

The **R in RAG, in ~150 lines of pure PyTorch.** No LangChain, no vector database,
no API keys, no model downloads — just `load -> chunk -> embed -> retrieve` built
from tensor ops you can read in one sitting.

```
Documents -> chunk_text() -> TF-IDF tensors -> cosine matmul -> top-k passages
```

## Why

Every RAG cheat sheet shows the same pipeline: loader, splitter, embeddings, vector
store, retriever. This repo implements that retrieval half with zero heavy
dependencies so you can see exactly what a "vector store" does: it's a normalized
matrix, and search is one `matrix @ query` followed by `torch.topk`.

At the scale of one book or one knowledge base, IDF-weighted lexical retrieval is
fast, transparent, and a strong baseline — and when it misses, you can see *why*
(see Limitations).

## Files

| File | What it does |
|---|---|
| `rag_lite/retriever.py` | Tokenizer, overlapping word-window chunker, TF-IDF vectorizer on torch tensors, cosine top-k search |
| `rag_lite/ollama_embed.py` | Same interface, neural embeddings via a local Ollama model (`nomic-embed-text`) |
| `compare_embedders.py` | Runs both backends over the same queries so you can see where each breaks |
| `demo_frameworks.py` | "Which storytelling framework fits my situation?" — semantic recommender over 9 classic communication frameworks |
| `demo_book.py` | Ask questions against **any** local `.pdf`/`.txt` and get the most relevant passages |
| `data/frameworks.json` | The 9 frameworks (Golden Circle, Minto Pyramid, ABT, …) with when-to-use and action steps |

## Quickstart

```bash
pip install torch pymupdf   # pymupdf only needed for PDF input
python demo_frameworks.py "I have one shot to pitch the board tomorrow"
python demo_book.py --doc your_book.pdf "when should I buy instead of build an agent"
```

## Real output (unedited)

```
$ python demo_frameworks.py "I have one shot to pitch the board tomorrow"

1. ABT: And, But, Therefore (Randy Olson)  (match 0.291)
   What: Shared context, a problem, then your solution - in exactly three beats.
   Do this: Write the ask as one sentence using and, but, therefore.

2. The StoryBrand Framework (Donald Miller)  (match 0.120)
3. Minto's Pyramid Principle (Barbara Minto)  (match 0.098)
```

```
$ python demo_book.py --doc "AI AGENTS.pdf" "when should I buy instead of build an agent" -k 2

Indexed 627 chunks from AI AGENTS.pdf
--- passage 1 (chunk 309, score 0.218) ---
...Use the five walls as the no-code-vs-code tripwire, and the honest team test:
will someone still be maintaining this in eighteen months? If not, lean buy or
no-code. Teams choose wrong for predictable reasons - hype, resume-building,
"we have engineers," and sunk cost...
```

(Book demo shown against *The Agent Decision* by Woongsik Su — bring your own
document; no book text is included in this repo.)

## How it works

1. **Chunk** — overlapping word windows (default 120 words, 30 overlap), so
   sentences straddling a boundary stay retrievable from both sides.
2. **Embed** — term-frequency vectors weighted by smoothed IDF
   (`log((1+N)/(1+df)) + 1`, same formula scikit-learn uses), L2-normalized.
3. **Store** — one dense `torch.Tensor` of shape `(n_chunks, vocab)`.
4. **Retrieve** — `scores = matrix @ query_vec` is cosine similarity (both sides
   normalized); `torch.topk` returns the passages.

## Two backends: lexical and neural

`TfidfRetriever` is the default — zero setup, no downloads. `OllamaRetriever`
is a drop-in with the identical `.search()` interface, backed by a local
embedding model. Still fully offline, still no API key.

```bash
ollama pull nomic-embed-text
python demo_frameworks.py --neural "we shipped late, time for the postmortem"
python demo_book.py --doc your_book.pdf --neural "when should I buy instead of build"
python compare_embedders.py        # head-to-head on the same corpus
```

### Measured difference (unedited output of `compare_embedders.py`)

| Query | TF-IDF picks | Neural picks |
|---|---|---|
| "our project failed and I need to run the postmortem" | StoryBrand ❌ (0.208) | **What, So What, Now What** ✅ (0.582) |
| "I have one shot to pitch the board tomorrow" | ABT ✅ (0.291) | ABT ✅ (0.539) |
| "I need my team to carry the message themselves" | StoryBrand ✅ (0.447) | StoryBrand ✅ (0.611) |
| "how do I open a status update for busy executives" | 3-Act ❌ (0.204) | ABT ~ (0.475) |

The first row is the whole argument for neural embeddings: "postmortem" and
"debrief" share no letters, so TF-IDF cannot connect them and picks a framework
that merely reuses more words. The embedding model connects them on meaning.

The last row is the honest counterweight — the ideal answer there is Minto's
Pyramid ("lead with the answer... senior audiences want the decision first").
Neural ranks it #2 at 0.471, a hair behind ABT; TF-IDF doesn't surface it in the
top 3 at all. Better, not solved.

## Limitations (honest ones)

- **TF-IDF is lexical.** Synonyms don't match — that's the postmortem row above.
  Use `--neural` when recall matters more than setup cost.
- **Neural costs an embedding call per chunk at index time.** Fine for a book
  (627 chunks, a couple of minutes on CPU); plan differently for a corpus.
- Dense matrix either way — fine for thousands of chunks, wasteful for millions.
- Retrieval-only: it finds passages, it doesn't write answers. Feed the passages
  to any LLM for the "G" in RAG.
rag-conversational-ai:
# RAG-Based Conversational AI System

Retrieval-Augmented Generation pipeline that answers questions over a custom document corpus with grounded, cited responses.

## What it does
- Ingests documents, chunks them, and builds an embeddings index (FAISS) for vector search
- Retrieves top-k relevant chunks per query and augments the LLM prompt (LangChain + LlamaIndex orchestration)
- Reaches 85% retrieval relevance on evaluation queries
- Sub-2-second end-to-end response latency via prompt engineering and inference optimization
- Deployed as containerized microservices with Docker and CI/CD

## Tech stack
Python, LangChain, LlamaIndex, OpenAI API, FAISS, Docker, FastAPI

## Architecture
1. Document loader and chunker
2. Embedding generation and FAISS vector store
3. Retriever with similarity search and re-ranking
4. LLM answer generation with source citations
5. REST API layer (FastAPI), containerized per service

## 🚀 Quick Start

```bash
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/sravanni369/ai-learning-repo.git
cd ai-learning-repo

# Create virtual environment
python -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate  # Linux/Mac
# venv\Scripts\activate   # Windows

# Install dependencies
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

## 📦 Requirements

Core dependencies include:
- **LLM clients**: `openai`, `anthropic`, `groq`, `google-generativeai`
- **Agent framework**: `pydantic-ai`, `langchain`, `llama-index`
- **Vector stores**: `faiss-cpu`, `chromadb`
- **ML/NLP**: `sentence-transformers`, `scikit-learn`, `numpy`, `pandas`
- **Observability**: `opentelemetry-sdk`

See [requirements.txt](requirements.txt) for the full list.
